content.title: Loading and Streaming the Experience
content.hook: A real application sometimes needs time.
content.context:
The mistake is pretending nothing is happening while the user waits.

Next.js provides route-level loading UI through `loading.tsx`.

Imagine:

```text
app/
  dashboard/
    loading.tsx
    page.tsx
```

The loading UI can appear while the route's work is being prepared.
goals: Master Loading and Streaming the Experience: “What should the user see while the system is not ready yet?”

content.question: What is the user experience problem with a route that shows nothing while waiting?

options.text: The user cannot tell whether the application is working.

feedback.correct: Correct answer: A. The user cannot tell whether the application is working.
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: A. The user cannot tell whether the application is working.

activities.title: Loading is part of the interface

content.title: Loading is part of the interface
content.text:
A loading state is not an afterthought.

It answers:

**“What should the user see while the system is not ready yet?”**

Good loading UI can preserve structure so the page feels stable.

activities.title: The shape should help the user predict

content.title: The shape should help the user predict
content.text:
A skeleton that resembles the eventual content can communicate:

“This space is reserved for something that is coming.”

That is often more useful than a generic spinner.

content.title: Streaming
content.text:
A framework can also reveal ready parts of the page while slower work continues.

The mental model:

```text
Ready content
   ↓
shown now
   +
slow content
   ↓
arrives later
```

options.text: Leave the user staring at a blank screen.
Provide meaningful route-level loading UI that communicates progress and preserves the page's shape.

feedback.correct: Correct answer: B. Provide meaningful route-level loading UI that communicates progress and preserves the page's shape.
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: B. Provide meaningful route-level loading UI that communicates progress and preserves the page's shape.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: Latency is part of UI design.
Do not only design the “happy final screen.”
Design what the user experiences **while the system is becoming ready**.
nextSteps: Take one route in an application and write the loading state you would want the user to see before its final content appears.

Complete the checkpoint and explain the mechanism in your own words. A wrong first prediction is expected; the mastery signal is whether you can explain the result and handle a changed case after feedback.

requirements: Screen-reader accessible code blocks and options
